To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
bounded word problems for group are complete under the uniform distribution.

(i) the bounded word problem for finitely generated groups is average-case NP-hard; (ii) the bounded word problems for finitely presented groups are average-case NP-hard, too; (iii) the bounded word and the word problems for groups are average-case complete for NP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: What is the complexity of the bounded word problem for a group G when its instances are chosen at a random?
the following question: how hard can a problem be, if it is chosen uniformly at random?
a new class of bounded problems for which average-case complexity can be analyzed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bounded word problems are average-case complete for groups.
the word problem for groups is average-case complete.
the bounded word problem for a group G is in average NP if and only if the group is finitely presented, and is in NP if and only it is finitely generated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, when given a word problem for a group, we cannot efficiently decide if it is solvable in polynomial time, even if the word problem is solvable on average.
bounded word problems for finitely presented groups are as hard as bounded word problems for context-free languages.

, in the average-case setting, the bounded word problem for a group is NP-complete if the group is given by a finite presentation, or if the group is finitely presented and the bound k is given by a constant, or if the bound k is a function of the length of a given word in the group.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when instances are chosen uniformly at random, the bounded word problem is average-case complete for groups.
, when the word problem is hard, there is no hope of obtaining an algorithm for it that is guaranteed to work in polynomial time.
, for groups, average-case hardness is not restricted to the special class of one-way functions.
